machine.title: CRISPY BITS TRIVIA
machine.defaultTickerText: CHOOSE A MODE • PULL THE LEVER • PICK A TOPIC • ANSWER THE QUESTION • DISCOVER THE CRISPY BITS •

questionPacks.description: The first editorially approved Crispy Bits Trivia question pack.

questions.question: On which planet does one rotation take longer than one trip around the Sun?
questions.explanation: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to rotate once, but only about 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun.
questions.crispyBit1: Venus rotates backwards compared with Earth and most other planets.
questions.crispyBit2: From Venus, the Sun would rise in the west and set in the east.
questions.whoaFact: Sunrise to sunset on Venus takes about 117 Earth days.
questions.sourceName: NASA Science — Venus Facts

questions.question: What colour was the Statue of Liberty when it was completed?
questions.explanation: The Statue’s exterior is copper. When completed in 1886 it was brown like a copper penny, not green.
questions.crispyBit1: The copper gradually oxidised and formed its famous green patina.
questions.crispyBit2: The National Park Service says the full colour change took roughly 25–30 years.
questions.whoaFact: The green patina helps protect the copper underneath from further weathering.
questions.sourceName: U.S. National Park Service — Statue of Liberty FAQ

questions.question: What can happen to the top of the Eiffel Tower on a sunny day?
questions.answerC: It moves slightly away from the Sun
questions.explanation: Sunlight heats one side of the iron structure more than the others, causing thermal expansion that makes the tower lean slightly away from the Sun.
questions.crispyBit1: Heat can also make the Eiffel Tower grow a few millimetres taller; cold makes it contract.
questions.crispyBit2: Wind moves the structure too — it was designed to withstand it.
questions.whoaFact: Over a clear day, the top can trace a roughly circular path about 15 centimetres across.
questions.sourceName: Eiffel Tower Official Site — Why the Tower Changes Size

questions.question: Which existed first?
questions.explanation: Oxford says there is evidence of teaching there by 1096, although the university has no single known foundation date.
questions.crispyBit1: Oxford developed rapidly after 1167, when Henry II banned English students from attending the University of Paris.
questions.crispyBit2: By around 1190, Oxford had its first known overseas student.
questions.whoaFact: Oxford was teaching students centuries before Leonardo da Vinci was born and before Gutenberg’s famous printing press appeared.
questions.sourceName: University of Oxford — Our History

questions.question: How long did the shortest war on record last?
questions.explanation: Guinness records the Anglo-Zanzibar War of 1896 as lasting from about 9:00 a.m. until 9:45 a.m. on 27 August.
questions.crispyBit1: Britain opposed the accession of Sultan Khalid after the previous sultan’s death.
questions.crispyBit2: British naval forces bombarded the palace and the confrontation was over before most feature films would finish.
questions.whoaFact: The entire war lasted about 45 minutes — shorter than many people’s commute.
questions.sourceName: Guinness World Records — Shortest War

questions.question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.explanation: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood through the gills and one pumps oxygenated blood around the body.
questions.crispyBit1: Octopus blood is blue because it uses copper-rich hemocyanin rather than iron-rich haemoglobin.
questions.crispyBit2: The main systemic heart stops beating when an octopus swims, helping explain why sustained swimming is exhausting.
questions.whoaFact: Much of an octopus’s nervous system is distributed through its arms, giving them remarkable local sensory and motor control.
questions.sourceName: Smithsonian Ocean — Octopuses, Squids and Relatives
questions.videoReason: Smithsonian visual companion directly demonstrates the octopus facts in the reveal.

questions.question: During Apollo 11’s lunar descent, the guidance computer repeatedly displayed which famous program alarm?
questions.explanation: Apollo 11 reported 1202 program alarms during descent. The computer was overloaded, but its priority system kept critical landing work running.
questions.crispyBit1: The Apollo Guidance Computer had about 2K words of erasable memory and 36K words of fixed memory.
questions.crispyBit2: Its software could discard lower-priority work when overloaded rather than simply stopping.
questions.whoaFact: During humanity’s first Moon landing, the computer protected the landing by shedding less-important work and continuing critical jobs.
questions.sourceName: NASA — Apollo 11 Lunar Surface Journal

questions.question: Much of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s permanent software was stored in what?
questions.explanation: Apollo’s fixed software was stored in magnetic core-rope memory, encoded by wires threaded through or around tiny magnetic cores.
questions.crispyBit1: Changing the finished software was nothing like editing a file — the memory ropes had to be physically manufactured.
questions.crispyBit2: Apollo’s final fixed-memory capacity grew to about 36K words.
questions.whoaFact: The software that helped take humans to the Moon literally existed in the physical routing of wires through magnetic cores.
questions.sourceName: NASA — Apollo Guidance Computer Oral History
questions.videoReason: Hands-on examination of real Apollo core-rope memory makes the physical-software concept tangible.

questions.question: Roughly how much total computer memory is distributed among the six computers aboard each Voyager spacecraft?
questions.explanation: NASA estimates the total memory among Voyager’s six computers at about 68 KB.
questions.crispyBit1: Voyager carries redundant pairs of three different computer types handling command, flight data and attitude control.
questions.crispyBit2: Voyager 1 launched in 1977 and became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space.
questions.whoaFact: With memory tiny by modern consumer standards, Voyager crossed the outer planets and has communicated from interstellar space.
questions.sourceName: NASA Science — Voyager FAQ

questions.question: The first prototype computer mouse built at SRI in 1964 was primarily made from what?
questions.explanation: Bill English built Douglas Engelbart’s first mouse prototype in 1964. Its casing was made from redwood.
questions.crispyBit1: The patent called it an “X-Y Position Indicator for a Display System,” not a mouse.
questions.crispyBit2: Engelbart’s team tested the mouse against other pointing methods and found it remarkably effective.
questions.whoaFact: The 1968 Mother of All Demos showed the mouse alongside hypertext, collaborative editing, windows and networked audio/video communication.
questions.sourceName: Computer History Museum — Original SRI Mouse
questions.videoTitle: 1968 Mother of All Demos with Doug Engelbart & Team (1/3)
questions.videoReason: Original remastered footage shows the mouse and foundational interface ideas being demonstrated.

questions.question: Before modern digital studios, how did Les Paul create many of his layered recordings?
questions.answerA: By playing multiple turntables at once
questions.answerB: By recording a performance, then playing along with it onto another recording
questions.answerC: By cutting several grooves into one record
questions.answerD: By routing microphones through a telephone exchange
questions.explanation: Les Paul recorded one layer to disc, played along with it while recording both to another disc, and repeated the process.
questions.crispyBit1: His recording of “Brazil” was assembled from nearly a dozen separate performances.
questions.crispyBit2: After Bing Crosby gave him an early commercial tape recorder, Paul modified it and continued experimenting on tape.
questions.whoaFact: Techniques pioneered by Les Paul helped make overdubbing and multitrack recording fundamental tools of modern record production.
questions.sourceName: Library of Congress — Les Paul: Inventing Modern Sound
questions.videoTitle: Les Paul: How Multi-track Recording Started
questions.videoReason: Museum interview material explains Les Paul's recording innovations in direct historical context.

questions.question: Which electronic instrument is normally played without the musician physically touching it?
questions.explanation: The theremin uses antennas and electromagnetic fields; the player moves their hands through the surrounding space to control pitch and volume.
questions.crispyBit1: Léon Theremin developed the instrument around 1920 and patented his design in the 1920s.
questions.crispyBit2: Lenin was reportedly so impressed that Theremin was sent touring Russia, Europe and the United States.
questions.whoaFact: Theremin was not only an electronic-music pioneer: Smithsonian notes that he also engaged in industrial espionage for the Soviet Union.
questions.sourceName: Smithsonian Magazine — The Soviet Spy Who Invented the Theremin
questions.videoTitle: Theremin - Clara Rockmore play The Swan (Saint-Saëns)
questions.videoReason: Historic Clara Rockmore performance immediately demonstrates touchless theremin performance.

questions.question: Charles Osborne holds the record for the longest recorded attack of hiccups. Roughly how long did it last?
questions.explanation: Charles Osborne began hiccupping in 1922 and continued until 1990 — 68 years.
questions.crispyBit1: He typically hiccupped around 20–40 times per minute.
questions.crispyBit2: He married twice, fathered eight children and led a largely normal life despite the condition.
questions.whoaFact: Guinness estimates Osborne hiccupped around 430 million times before the attack finally stopped.
questions.sourceName: Guinness World Records — Longest Attack of Hiccups

questions.question: French entertainer Michel Lotito became famous for eating which of these?
questions.explanation: Michel Lotito, nicknamed Monsieur Mangetout, consumed a Cessna 150 piece by piece as part of his extraordinary metal-eating career.
questions.crispyBit1: His menu also included bicycles, shopping trolleys, televisions and other metal objects.
questions.crispyBit2: He cut objects into small pieces and swallowed them with mineral oil and water.
questions.whoaFact: Guinness estimates Lotito ate more than nine tonnes of metal, while ordinary foods such as bananas and hard-boiled eggs reportedly gave him indigestion.
questions.sourceName: Guinness World Records — Monsieur Mangetout
questions.videoTitle: The Man With The Strangest Diet...
questions.videoReason: Official Guinness video about Michel Lotito directly extends the airplane-eating reveal.

questions.question: In 1919, Boston was struck by a deadly flood of what?
questions.explanation: A huge storage tank ruptured in Boston’s North End, releasing about 2.3 million gallons of molasses.
questions.crispyBit1: The wave was reported to be around 15 feet high.
questions.crispyBit2: Despite the phrase “slow as molasses,” the wave raced through the area at up to about 35 mph.
questions.whoaFact: The disaster killed 21 people and the wave was powerful enough to damage buildings and knock a firehouse from its foundations.
questions.sourceName: Smithsonian Magazine — The Great Molasses Flood

questions.question: In Strasbourg in 1518, hundreds of people reportedly became caught up in an outbreak of what?
questions.explanation: Historical accounts describe a dancing mania in Strasbourg in 1518 that eventually involved large numbers of people.
questions.crispyBit1: Authorities reportedly provided spaces and musicians because they believed sufferers needed to dance it out.
questions.crispyBit2: Explanations have included ergot poisoning and collective psychological distress, but the precise nature of the episode remains debated.
questions.whoaFact: The authorities’ response to an apparent epidemic of uncontrollable dancing included encouraging more dancing with professional musicians.
questions.sourceName: Smithsonian Magazine — Dancing Mania

questions.question: Which animal naturally produces cube-shaped poo?
questions.explanation: Bare-nosed wombats really do produce roughly cube-shaped droppings, shaped by the mechanics of their intestines.
questions.crispyBit1: A wombat can produce scores of cubes in a day.
questions.crispyBit2: Scientists think the shape may help droppings stay where wombats place them when marking territory instead of rolling away.
questions.whoaFact: Researchers estimate the material experiences around 40,000 intestinal contractions as the cube shape develops.
questions.sourceName: Smithsonian Magazine — Why Wombats Poop Cubes

questions.question: What happens to a wood frog’s heart during its frozen winter hibernation?
questions.explanation: Wood frogs can survive while much of their bodies freezes. During this state they stop breathing and their hearts stop beating.
questions.crispyBit1: Their livers produce large amounts of glucose that helps protect cells as ice forms around them.
questions.crispyBit2: Even their eyes can freeze and turn white.
questions.whoaFact: They can spend winter with no heartbeat or breathing; in spring the heart starts again, then brain activity returns and finally the legs move.
questions.sourceName: U.S. National Park Service — Wood Frog Biological Miracle
questions.videoTitle: This frog literally freezes itself to survive the winter
questions.videoReason: National Geographic footage visually demonstrates the wood frog's freeze-survival adaptation.

questions.question: During the Cold War, what animal did the CIA surgically equip with listening equipment to spy on conversations?
questions.explanation: Beginning in 1964, the CIA explored using a cat fitted with a microphone, transmitter and antenna to monitor conversations.
questions.crispyBit1: A microphone was implanted in one ear, a transmitter under the skin and an antenna woven into the fur.
questions.crispyBit2: The technology worked, but the cat could not reliably be made to go where the CIA wanted.
questions.whoaFact: The famous story that the spy cat was immediately killed by a taxi is a myth; the CIA says the equipment was removed and the cat was unharmed.
questions.sourceName: CIA — Natural Spies: Animals in Espionage

questions.question: During World War II, psychologist B. F. Skinner proposed guiding missiles using what?
questions.explanation: Skinner’s Project Pigeon trained pigeons to peck at an image of a target so their responses could guide a weapon.
questions.crispyBit1: The proposed nose cone contained three pigeon compartments looking toward the target.
questions.crispyBit2: This was not just a joke on paper: Skinner trained birds and built experimental hardware.
questions.whoaFact: An actual three-pigeon guidance nose cone survives in the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History.
questions.sourceName: Smithsonian — B.F. Skinner’s Pigeon-Guided Missile Nose Cone

questions.question: In Australia’s famous 1932 “Emu War”, what weapon was deployed against the birds?
questions.explanation: Military personnel were deployed in Western Australia with Lewis machine guns after large numbers of emus damaged crops.
questions.crispyBit1: The birds repeatedly scattered into smaller groups, making them remarkably difficult targets.
questions.crispyBit2: Mechanical problems and rough terrain made the operation far less effective than expected.
questions.whoaFact: The episode became famous because military machine guns were genuinely deployed against fast-moving emus — and the birds proved extremely difficult to control.
questions.sourceName: National Museum of Australia — Emu War
questions.videoTitle: The Great Emu War: how it started and who won
questions.videoReason: Official ABC Australia explainer provides strong local historical context for the Emu War.

questions.question: During World War II, Britain seriously explored building a gigantic aircraft carrier primarily from what?
questions.explanation: Project Habakkuk proposed an enormous carrier made from pykrete — ice reinforced with wood fibre.
questions.crispyBit1: The concept envisioned a structure vastly larger than conventional aircraft carriers.
questions.crispyBit2: A prototype was actually built on Patricia Lake in Canada.
questions.whoaFact: Governments seriously investigated whether a refrigerated floating mass of reinforced ice could serve as an enormous wartime aircraft platform.
questions.sourceName: Parks Canada — Project Habakkuk

questions.question: In 1976, a confrontation in the Korean DMZ that killed two U.S. Army officers began over work on what?
questions.explanation: A United Nations Command work party was trimming a poplar tree in the Joint Security Area when North Korean soldiers attacked, killing two U.S. officers.
questions.crispyBit1: Three days later, Operation Paul Bunyan returned with engineers, chainsaws and overwhelming military support.
questions.crispyBit2: The operation was designed to remove the tree while demonstrating that interference would carry enormous risk.
questions.whoaFact: A tree-trimming dispute escalated into a major military show of force — and ended with the poplar cut down to a stump.
questions.sourceName: U.S. Army — Operation Paul Bunyan

questions.question: After experimenting with a spy cat, the CIA later developed a robotic version of which animal?
questions.explanation: CIA engineers developed unmanned underwater vehicles disguised as catfish, named Charlie and Charlene.
questions.crispyBit1: The robotic fish could control speed and depth and communicate by radio.
questions.crispyBit2: One proposed use was collecting water samples for signs of nuclear runoff or biochemical agents.
questions.whoaFact: The CIA’s own account jokes that Charlie could find out whether anything “fishy” was going on.
questions.sourceName: CIA — Natural Spies: Animals in Espionage

questions.question: What piece of technology helped police finally identify the BTK killer Dennis Rader?
questions.explanation: In 2005 Rader sent investigators a computer disk. Recoverable information on it helped point investigators toward Dennis Rader and a Wichita church.
questions.crispyBit1: Rader had spent years sending taunting communications to authorities and media.
questions.crispyBit2: The disk’s metadata became an important investigative lead connecting the communications to Rader.
questions.whoaFact: After avoiding identification for decades, Rader helped expose himself by sending investigators digital information on a floppy disk.
questions.sourceName: FBI — Kansas City Field Office History

questions.question: Which technique helped investigators identify the Golden State Killer decades after his crimes?
questions.explanation: Investigators combined crime-scene DNA with genetic genealogy to build family connections and narrow the suspect pool before confirmatory DNA testing.
questions.crispyBit1: The suspect himself did not need to have uploaded his DNA to a genealogy service for relatives’ matches to create leads.
questions.crispyBit2: Investigators used discarded material associated with Joseph DeAngelo for confirmatory comparison.
questions.whoaFact: A family tree can become a forensic map: distant genetic matches can help investigators work toward the identity of an unknown suspect.
questions.sourceName: National Institute of Justice — Investigative Genetic Genealogy

questions.question: What ultimately provided the crucial lead that identified the Unabomber, Ted Kaczynski?
questions.explanation: After the Unabomber’s manifesto was published, David Kaczynski recognised similarities to his brother Ted’s ideas and writing and contacted authorities.
questions.crispyBit1: David supplied earlier writings by his brother for comparison.
questions.crispyBit2: Investigators found distinctive similarities in language, phrasing and ideas that helped support the case for a search warrant.
questions.whoaFact: After years of avoiding conventional forensic identification, Kaczynski’s own writing style became part of the trail that led investigators to him.
questions.sourceName: FBI — Unabomber

questions.question: How long did the Zodiac Killer’s famous 340-character cipher remain unsolved?
questions.explanation: The 340-character cipher was mailed in 1969 and solved in 2020 by an international team of private codebreakers; the FBI verified the solution.
questions.crispyBit1: The team was David Oranchak, Jarl Van Eycke and Australian mathematician Sam Blake.
questions.crispyBit2: Blake worked from Melbourne and used the University of Melbourne’s Spartan computing resources.
questions.whoaFact: They cracked a cipher that had resisted solution for 51 years — but the decoded message still did not reveal Zodiac’s identity.
questions.sourceName: ABC News Australia — Zodiac Cipher Solved
questions.videoTitle: Let's Crack Zodiac — Episode 5 — The 340 Is Solved!
questions.videoReason: First-person explanation by one of the three codebreakers who solved Z340.

questions.question: In the investigation that led to a landmark murder case using DNA profiling, what did DNA do first?
questions.answerC: Cleared a suspect who had confessed
questions.explanation: DNA profiling showed that Richard Buckland, who had confessed to one killing, was not the source of the crime-scene DNA.
questions.crispyBit1: Police later conducted a mass DNA-screening operation involving thousands of local men.
questions.crispyBit2: Colin Pitchfork tried to evade screening by getting another man to provide a sample in his place; the deception was later exposed.
questions.whoaFact: One of forensic DNA’s defining early achievements was not catching someone — it was proving that a confessed suspect was not the killer.
questions.sourceName: Guinness World Records — First Use of DNA Profiling to Clear a Criminal Suspect

questions.question: What mundane clue helped police identify “Son of Sam” killer David Berkowitz in 1977?
questions.explanation: Investigators traced parking summonses issued near the scene of the final shooting and found Berkowitz’s vehicle among them.
questions.crispyBit1: A witness had noticed activity involving a car being ticketed near the area.
questions.crispyBit2: That ordinary administrative record helped investigators focus on Berkowitz.
questions.whoaFact: One of New York’s most intense manhunts was cracked in part by something spectacularly ordinary: a parking ticket.
questions.sourceName: The Washington Post — Son of Sam
